status: completed relevance and independent occurrence-evidence review

review.requirement_proposition: AI actors should provide meaningful information making stakeholders aware of interactions with AI, including workplace interactions.

previous_canonical_assessment.applicability_basis: Section 1.3(ii) addresses awareness of interactions with AI. Human-controlled accounts used static generated/manipulated portraits; the sources do not describe a recipient interacting with an AI participant. AI imagery is a provenance concern, but is not itself the represented interaction-awareness object. AI-phase dates are also unknown.

review.reason_for_change: The preserved object is a static military-ID or profile/likeness representation created and used by people. No autonomous AI participant or actual interaction with the generation system by the victim is established. Source-origin deception is distinct from the specific AI-interaction-awareness proposition.

review.requirement_proposition: Protect vulnerable users, require specific consent for bounded deceptive styles, document emergent deception and define safeguard-failure protocols.

previous_withheld_assessment.applicability_basis: The Welsh settlement describes a 2022–2026 catfishing campaign with later synthetic images; exact AI-use dates and generation methods are unresolved. For IEEE-7014.1 6.7.3(l-p), the missing applicability fact is whether the operator adopted IEEE 7014.1 for an emulated-empathy GPAI partner in the interaction and the applicable vulnerable-user or deceptive-style safeguard context; impersonation imagery or task deception alone does not establish a human–AI partnering undertaking. Taxonomy correspondence does not supply these scope facts; no occurrence-level requirement finding is recorded.

review.reason_for_change: 6.7.3(l-p) governs partner-based/emulated-empathy vulnerability/style safeguards or emotional-data consent. These human-directed facial-composite, static-ID, executive-profile or social-profile impersonations do not instantiate the partner-system/affective consent object. For the 2024/2025 occurrences the 2026 source also postdates the event.

review.requirement_proposition: AI actors should respect the rule of law, human rights and democratic and human-centred values throughout the AI lifecycle, including non-discrimination, equality, freedom, dignity, individual autonomy, privacy and data protection, diversity, fairness, social justice and internationally recognised labour rights.
review.reason_for_change: The solicitor and agreed statement establish unauthorised AI-edited/generated identifiable depictions within a 2022-2026 impersonation campaign, directly engaging autonomy/privacy/dignity. However, the first AI-image date and timing of particular depictions relative to the May 2024 OECD version are not preserved. The post-publication external finding remains Boundary rather than attributing the entire earlier campaign to AI or applying the later version retrospectively.

review.requirement_proposition: Add intended purpose, nominal operator and responsible contact information to the public documentation.

previous_canonical_assessment.applicability_basis: IEEE 7001 Table 2 level 3 concerns autonomous-system public/bystander transparency. The established campaign involves a human operator deploying static AI depictions through social accounts, not an autonomous participant. Content provenance is distinct from identification and public documentation of an autonomous system.

review.reason_for_change: Table 2 level 3 concerns autonomous-system identification or public purpose/operator/contact documentation. A human-directed static ID/profile image or unidentified impersonation medium is not an established autonomous-system interaction or the generation system's documentation activity.

review.requirement_proposition: Parties must ensure adequate transparency requirements tailored to the context and risk of AI lifecycle activities, including identification of AI-generated content.

previous_canonical_assessment.applicability_basis: Article 8 addresses Parties and their territorial implementation of the Convention. The the 2022–2026 Davies impersonation campaign evidence establishes neither entry into force for the relevant Party nor implementation covering the private actor’s activity. Signature, a civil settlement or corporate fraud disclosure does not supply those applicability facts.

review.reason_for_change: Article 8 governs a treaty Party's implementation of transparency/contestability duties. The private perpetrators, companies or bank-verification applications identify no commenced relevant Party implementation/territorial duty.

review.requirement_proposition: Do not apply affective modeling to identifiable subject data without prior informed consent.

previous_withheld_assessment.applicability_basis: The Welsh settlement describes a 2022–2026 catfishing campaign with later synthetic images; exact AI-use dates and generation methods are unresolved. For IEEE-7014 4.3.5.2(d), the missing applicability fact is whether the developer undertook IEEE 7014 for an emulated-empathy system applying affective modelling to identifiable subject affective data; image depiction, face swapping or identity matching does not by itself establish affective modelling, and the anonymous-data exception cannot be resolved without that processing scope. Taxonomy correspondence does not supply these scope facts; no occurrence-level requirement finding is recorded.

review.reason_for_change: 4.3.5.2(d) prohibits unconsented affective modelling of identifiable data. Identity likeness transformation is not evidence of modelling a subject's emotions/affect; the technical subject matter differs.

review.requirement_proposition: Make the system clearly identifiable as autonomous to users and bystanders.

review.requirement_proposition: Parties must seek to ensure that people interacting with AI are told they are interacting with a system rather than a human, as appropriate to the context.

review.reason_for_change: Article 15(2) governs a treaty Party's implementation of transparency/contestability duties. The private perpetrators, companies or bank-verification applications identify no commenced relevant Party implementation/territorial duty.

review.requirement_proposition: Do not place, put into service or use AI that deploys subliminal, purposefully manipulative or deceptive techniques causing materially distorted behavior and significant harm.

previous_withheld_assessment.applicability_basis: The Welsh catfishing campaign is reported to have continued from 2022 into 2026, with AI-generated or manipulated images used later in the campaign. The record does not date that AI use relative to 2 February 2025 and does not identify an EU-market provider, Union-established deployer, or output used in the Union. The duration and Article 2 nexus therefore prevent a definitive applicability decision.

review.reason_for_change: The registered 2026-07-27 source version (Article 5(1)(a)) postdates the reported application/phishing/transfer/impersonation occurrence. No later report or settlement retrospectively supplies the defined territorial high-risk/prohibition conditions.

review.requirement_proposition: Minimise data and make review, modification and withdrawal of consent immediate and accessible.

previous_withheld_assessment.applicability_basis: The Welsh settlement describes a 2022–2026 catfishing campaign with later synthetic images; exact AI-use dates and generation methods are unresolved. For IEEE-7014.1 6.22.3(a-b), the missing applicability fact is whether the developer or platform operator adopted IEEE 7014.1 for a partner-based GPAI system using emulated empathy and collecting personal, emotional, memory or relationship-history data in this occurrence; public output or stored task content alone does not establish that partnering and consent-control scope. Taxonomy correspondence does not supply these scope facts; no occurrence-level requirement finding is recorded.

review.reason_for_change: 6.22.3(a-b) governs partner-based/emulated-empathy vulnerability/style safeguards or emotional-data consent. These human-directed facial-composite, static-ID, executive-profile or social-profile impersonations do not instantiate the partner-system/affective consent object. For the 2024/2025 occurrences the 2026 source also postdates the event.

review.requirement_proposition: Document interactions with GAI systems to users prior to interactive activities, particularly in contexts involving more significant risks.

previous_canonical_assessment.applicability_basis: GV-5.1-002 addresses users before interactive GAI activities. This human-directed account campaign deployed static depictions; no recipient-side interactive GAI activity is established. The operator’s unpublished generation requests are separate and not substituted for the occurrence pathway.

review.reason_for_change: The action documents GAI interactions to users before interactive activity. The observed object is a static image/profile, with no victim interaction with the generation system or identified interactive GAI participant; the specific user-interaction documentation scope is absent.

conclusion_change.previous: Weston had access to Davies’s identifiable photographs and later used AI-generated or edited depictions of her without consent to sustain a false social identity. Possession of those photographs did not authorise making new person-bound portrayals. The settlement and party-side account support that requester-side identity authority failure; they do not reveal the generator, show an autonomous AI objective or establish that every consequence arose in the later AI phase. The agreed responsibility and unauthorised identifiable AI depictions support requester-side identity and deception mechanisms, but the AI phase’s start and contribution to individual consequences remain unknown. A false social persona carrying static images is distinct from an autonomous or interactive GAI participant. No requirement finding is attributed to the whole four-year campaign.
conclusion_change.new: Weston had access to Davies’s identifiable photographs and later used AI-generated or edited depictions of her without consent to sustain a false social identity. Possession of those photographs did not authorise making new person-bound portrayals. The settlement and party-side account support that requester-side identity authority failure; they do not reveal the generator, show an autonomous AI objective or establish that every consequence arose in the later AI phase. The agreed responsibility and unauthorised identifiable AI depictions support requester-side identity and deception mechanisms, but the AI phase’s start and contribution to individual consequences remain unknown. A false social persona carrying static images is distinct from an autonomous or interactive GAI participant. No requirement finding is attributed to the whole four-year campaign. Independent external assessment retains a Boundary for the post-publication OECD autonomy/privacy/dignity proposition because the AI phase's timing is unpreserved. Static-profile identity misuse does not establish autonomous/interactive-system or affective-modelling requirements.
